title: Joel Barlow to James Monroe, Paris, 25 September 1812, and to the Duke of Bassano, 25 October 1812 (NARA M34 roll 16): two passages in the Paris legation code of 1811-1813 (the = 1700) that carry no decipherment, read in part with a key rebuilt from ten letters deciphered at the time

documents.shelfmark: NARA RG 59, Despatches from US Ministers to France, vol. 13, microfilm M34 roll 16, frame 0232 (right page) and frame 0233
documents.route: Joel Barlow (US minister to France), Paris -> James Monroe, Secretary of State, Washington

plaintext.source: No decipherment on the film (all 296 frames of roll 16 surveyed, October 2026). Not found in print (print check of 21 Nov 2026, NOTES.md section 8); Barlow's private letter to Madison of the next day, on the same matters, is printed with Madison's decipherment in The Papers of James Madison, Presidential Series 5:354-57.

plaintext.source: American State Papers, Foreign Relations 3:604 prints a two-paragraph extract of the note without the coded sentences (also Wait's State Papers, 1819, 9:218-19, and Todd, Life and Letters of Joel Barlow, 1886, pp. 270-71). No decipherment on the film. The note Bassano received, presumably in clear, would be in the French foreign ministry archives (Correspondance politique, Etats-Unis, vol. 69 f. 350, cited by Brant 1958), not digitised.

transcription.source: NARA M34 roll 16 frames 0240-0241 (copy A) and 0246-0247 (copy B), full-resolution catalogue JPEGs
transcription.notes: Copy A 46 code numbers, copy B 47, each read by three or four AI readers (October 2026; two blind readers and, for copy A, a full-text transcriber, 21 Nov 2026). The two copies differ in the code in four places (transcription headers); where a digit of one copy is unclear the other copy is cited. system.summary: The numerical code of the United States legation in Paris, 1811-1813: words and syllables as numbers from 7 to 1700 (the = 1700, of = 631, and = 513, to = 494), written among clear words. Used by Barlow, by Monroe and Madison writing to him, and by Thomas Barlow after his uncle's death. No key sheet is known; 623 numbers are rebuilt here from ten letters deciphered at the time.
system.notes: distinct_symbols = distinct numbers in the three transcription files together. In the 25 September letter a comma joins the numbers of one word and a dash separates words; in the Bassano copies the numbers are separated by spaces only. I and J are one letter, U and V one letter. Homophones: several syllables have more than one number (ti: 133 and, in copy A, 103). unread_groups = 163, the one number left bare in the readings; eight more numbers (seven words) are read from the sense and marked [?].

prior_solution.where: No decipherment on the film. Print check of 21 Nov 2026: the 25 Sep 1812 despatch is not printed (American State Papers Foreign Relations 3; Wait's State Papers 1819; Todd 1886; The Papers of James Monroe vol. 6); the note to Bassano is printed only as an extract that stops before the coded sentences (ASP FR 3:604; Wait 9:218-19; Todd pp. 270-71). Brant, William and Mary Quarterly 15 (1958) pp. 447-48, gives the context of the coded clause from the French archives (the eighty-licence proposal) and cites the note as received (AAE, CP Etats-Unis 69 f. 350) without quoting it; he also reports that the French foreign ministry intercepted and partly deciphered Barlow's letter to Madison of 26 Sep 1812 (CP 68 f. 346). Exact-phrase searches of Founders Online, Internet Archive, HathiTrust and Google Books found nothing. Not read page by page: Brant 1961, Hill 2005, Egan 1983, Buel 2011 (loan-only). No published table of this code found (Weber 1979 p. 187 gives one decoded sentence of a 1813 letter).

conditions.human_role: Andrew Beling set the tasks and the rules (second readings made without sight of the first, with pass marks written beforehand). AI agents located the sources, transcribed, aligned, checked, reviewed and wrote. No person has read the numbers or the readings against the images.
tools: decode.py (this folder): applies key.tsv and proposals.tsv to the transcriptions and checks the decryption files

solution.what: Andrew Beling contribution: all 296 frames of NARA M34 roll 16 surveyed; coded text found on frames 11, 232-233, 240-247, 249-250, 291-295; the State Department's separate decipherment of the 29 Sep 1811 despatch found on frames 15-16.

Andrew Beling contribution: 436 numbers rebuilt from the M34 frames: the clerk's writing between the lines on frames 242-295 and a word-for-word alignment of frame 11 (503 numbers) with its decipherment. The three passages without a decipherment then read at 78% of their numbers.

Andrew Beling contribution: four more letters in the same code, deciphered between the lines at the time, added from the Library of Congress (Monroe to Barlow 16 Jun 1812; Madison to Barlow 11 Aug 1812; Barlow to Madison 26 Sep 1812) and a sale photograph (Monroe to Barlow 23 Apr 1812, last page): 655 numbers.

Andrew Beling contribution: every source re-read by two AI readers each who had not seen the first reading (no person), pass marks written first (95% per reader, 98% for either). 3,297 numbers compared; 56 misread numbers corrected (32 in Barlow to Madison 26 Sep 1812, 16 in Madison to Barlow 11 Aug 1812), 22 marked doubtful; nine of fourteen sources missed a mark (two through the first transcription's errors, two through poor film, five short passages by one to four numbers). Table after correction: 649 numbers, of which 623 have a value from a decipherer of the time and 21 a word.

Andrew Beling contribution: the two letters transcribed in full and written out as sentences. 25 Sep 1812: 59 of 64 numbers read from the key, four words completed from the sense ([?indemnities], [?making], [?progress], [?indemnity]), one whole-word number written like 1780 marked [?the], and one number left unread ([163]th June). Bassano: 42 of 46 (copy A) and 44 of 47 (copy B); three words completed from the sense ([?little], [?determined], [?regard]); 'justice', 'of' and the full 'Imperial' taken from copy B where copy A is short.

Andrew Beling contribution: two further AI agents that had made none of the readings checked the folder. A verifier applied the key with its own script (same counts and sentences) and read the 157 numbers on the frames (144 by shape; the other 13 are the blotted or miswritten ones listed in the transcription headers). A second agent of ours, acting as reviewer, read all 157 numbers by shape before opening the folder (153 agree), read the decryptions as sentences and found both coherent with scattered holes (its own grade A, not recorded as a reading_review, which is the repository reviewer's to give); the four changes it asked for were made.

gaps.item: 815 (twice), 1567, 1404 (25 Sep); 624, 706, 103 (Bassano): seven numbers with no value in any decipherment of the time
gaps.detail: each occurs only in these passages; each has a value from the sense (proposals.tsv), marked [?] in the readings. More letters in this code would settle them: Eustis to Barlow, 25 Sep 1812 (catalogue 770, Clements Library, not digitised); the second copy of Monroe to Barlow, 16 Jun 1812 (lead 1279, Princeton); the note Bassano received (French foreign ministry archives, CP Etats-Unis 69 f. 350); the French decipherment of Barlow's letter of 26 Sep 1812 (CP 68 f. 346).

texts.label: Barlow to Monroe, Paris, 25 Sep 1812, M34 roll 16 frames 0232R-0233
texts.summary: Barlow reports that indemnities for past spoliations are at last under discussion on a footing more favorable than he expected, that his note of June has convinced everyone in the imperial confidence, that the Emperor's decision is expected in a few days, and that the treaty will meet no difficulty once the mode of indemnity is agreed.

reading_review.by: integration review of PR #878 (AI agent, for the maintainers); not a person
reading_review.note: Read here as sentences: reading_1812-09-25.md against the unedited decryption_1812-09-25.txt, line by line. Coherent English throughout; the coded paragraph (indemnities for past spoliations under discussion, the men in the imperial confidence convinced, the Emperor's decision expected, the treaty to follow once the mode of indemnity is agreed) reads as plain prose with every hole marked. Grade B rather than A because 9 of the 34 coded words are holes (reviewer recount in rounds 4 and 5: 25 of 34 sure), among them the key noun 'indemnities' twice, 'making progress' and the day in June (163). The round-4 review compared the 64 numbers with NARA M34 roll 16 frame 0232; that was not repeated here. Not checked: the ten key-source letters against their images, the single-occurrence key values; docs/_validate.py not run.

texts.label: Barlow to the Duke of Bassano, Paris, 25 Oct 1812 (copy A, M34 roll 16 frames 0240-0241; copy B frames 0246-0247)
texts.summary: Accepting Bassano's invitation to Wilna, Barlow warns that if the project (the treaty of commerce and the convention of indemnities), whose execution would cost the imperial treasury little or nothing, is rejected, the President can see in it nothing but a determined refusal of justice on the part of his Imperial Majesty, which must embarrass the American government in its operations in regard to England as well as France.
